svg.text: Falling conscious level: what changes first, and what it means
Glasgow Coma Scale — three separate scores, always reported separately
A total of 9 can be three different patients. E2V2M5 and E4V1M4 are not the same problem. Report all three.
The earliest sign is the one people miss
The FIRST change in rising intracranial
pressure is a change in CONSCIOUS LEVEL —
often just new restlessness, drowsiness or
Pupil changes and bradycardia come LATE.
Waiting for a blown pupil is waiting too long.
Cushing's triad — a late, pre-terminal sign
Widening pulse pressure with bradycardia is
the brainstem being compressed. This is an
emergency, not an observation to chart.
Nursing actions that lower intracranial pressure
Head of bed up 30 degrees · head and neck in MIDLINE — a turned head kinks the jugular vein and
blocks venous drainage · avoid hip flexion · space out care, since suction and turning both raise pressure
· treat pain and fever · avoid straining, coughing and constipation.
Do NOT lie the patient flat, and do NOT restrict fluids to the point of hypotension — the brain needs
perfusion pressure. Cerebral perfusion = mean arterial pressure MINUS intracranial pressure.
